meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board approved a permit for the Eagle House supporters' fall fundraiser, welcomed a new Principal Assessor, and spent most of the meeting preparing for Thursday's special town meeting: it recommended a lower, "net" figure than the school committee requested for the article supplementing the FY27 school budget with additional state aid, and worked through how to fund a separate citizen petition article restoring cut middle school and some high school sports. The board voted to create a special revenue fund from one-time Winter Recovery Assistance Program money to serve as that sports article's funding source after using most of the RAP funds to close the FY26 snow and ice deficit. It also voted to send an amended letter to state legislative leaders supporting the voter-approved audit of the Massachusetts legislature.

meetings.summary: The Finance Committee held a public hearing on three warrant articles for a citizen-petitioned special town meeting, driven by new state aid the town received after the legislature's final budget exceeded the governor's January figure. The committee voted to recommend approval of article 1 (a school spending plan funded by that new state aid, including a second grade teacher, reading specialist, assistant principal, music teacher, literacy support, and reduced athletic transportation costs) and voted to defer articles 2 and 3 to town meeting itself, since article 2's petitioner plans to move to pass it over and article 3's funding source (a possible new special-purpose fund drawn from RAP money) had not yet been established by the Select Board or ratified by the School Committee. The committee also approved prior minutes, heard committee reports, and decided to caucus informally at town meeting rather than hold a separate pre-town-meeting session.

The committee deferred the second warrant article to town meeting itself, since its own petitioner plans to move to pass it over.

The committee also deferred the third article, covering middle and high school sports funding, because its funding source had not yet been established by the Select Board or ratified by the School Committee.

Town officials informally agreed to apply a school choice credit to reduce the amount needed for the sports-funding article, pending action by the Select Board and School Committee the following week.

meetings.headline: Select Board unanimously ruled the dog is not a nuisance after a hearing where no witness reported evidence of nuisance behavior.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board held a public hearing under MGL c.140 §157 on a nuisance-dog complaint filed by George and Jennifer Burden against neighbors Charles and Stacy Cordmash. meetings.summary: The Select Board, joined by the Facilities Director and members of the Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee, conducted an on-site walking tour of Brooks House and the former TCP school building to observe their physical condition ahead of any future public deliberation on the properties. what_happened.line: Select Board members, the facilities director, and the town's building design committee toured Brooks House and the former TCP school in person to assess condition.
A food pantry representative questioned whether Brooks House can hold the pantry, citing water, bathroom, and floor-load needs, with no alternative site ready by October 1st.
The tour covered TCP's boiler leaks, asbestos-related ceiling costs, and ADA-trigger cost thresholds on roof work, with several cost figures described as estimates still to be confirmed.
A board member asked what basis existed for a roof-cost figure presented at a 2023 special town meeting; the facilities director said no formal roofer estimate existed at that time.
No votes were taken on the properties; the meeting ended with a vote to adjourn.

why_it_matters: Any eventual decision on Brooks House or TCP — including where the food pantry operates — will carry repair, ADA-compliance, and asbestos-abatement costs that a future town meeting may be asked to fund.
Whether roof or renovation work crosses an ADA-trigger cost threshold changes the scope and cost of any project at TCP, which affects what gets proposed to voters.
The pantry's relocation options remain unresolved, which matters to anyone who relies on that service or lives near either building.

meetings.summary: A joint Select Board / Lunenburg Municipal Building Design Committee meeting opened with a presentation on Mass Save energy-summit incentives for building electrification, then shifted to a long workshop on the deteriorating TC Pacios (TCP) building — its failing systems, a history of a double-appropriated roof-repair fund later corrected at town meeting, and whether to repair or demolish it. No formal vote was taken on TCP or the Brooks House, but the group leaned toward not investing further in TCP, tasked the Facilities Director with cost estimates, and agreed the committee will bring formal recommendations on both buildings to a future meeting, with its next meeting set for August 3rd.

The board also approved the September 1 state primary election warrant and ratified the DPW collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Local 170, then adjourned to meet again the next evening in a joint workshop with the Municipal Building Design Committee.

minutes.headline: Select Board moves toward a decision on demolishing or renovating the deteriorating TCP building

what_happened.line: The board set a path toward deciding whether to demolish or renovate the deteriorating TCP building, asking the Municipal Building Design Committee for a formal recommendation to feed fall capital planning.
The board directed staff to draft its overdue, town-meeting-directed report on selling or long-term leasing the Brooks House, targeted for completion by the fall town meeting.

The Finance Committee and Select Board approved FY2026 year-end transfers, covering legal expenses, the sealer of weights and measures, and town report printing, drawn from a vacant planning board salary line.
The board voted to approve the Town Manager's proposed FY27 goals, including a review of outsourcing payroll processing and work toward adopting several tabled financial policies.

why_it_matters: Whichever way the TCP decision goes, the cost was described as able to consume most or all of a year's capital plan, which shapes what other town projects can be funded that year.
The Brooks House report determines the town's public path for a building it has been directed by town meeting to resolve, and residents may see options at a future town meeting.
Financial policies under discussion -- OPEB funding, reserves, and revenue projections -- bear on the town's long-term borrowing capacity and, eventually, the tax rate.

meetings.headline: The board took the Flatill Road bridge land by eminent domain and tabled the DPW union contract over legal disputes.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified a police detective promotion and several routine appointments, heard a lengthy planning-director update and a historical society pitch for a Revolutionary War memorial, and got tangled in a dispute over a stalled Trust Fund Commission appointment. It also acted on several money and process items — adopting the IRS mileage rate, taking an eminent-domain easement for the Flatill Road bridge, designating the Cable Advisory Committee as special municipal employees, choosing police over a constable for three upcoming elections, and approving minutes including newly released executive-session employment agreements — while tabling the DPW union contract, the special election warrant, and the trust fund appointment, and deferring a decision on a special town meeting for additional state education funding.

minutes.headline: The board took the Flatill Road bridge land by eminent domain and tabled the DPW union contract over legal disputes.

what_happened.line: The board tabled ratification of the new DPW union contract after labor counsel flagged discrepancies to resolve.
The board voted to take a temporary easement at 890 Flatill Road by eminent domain to keep the bridge project moving.
A dispute over how the town processed Richard Howard's Trust Fund Commission application went unresolved, with the appointment pushed to a future agenda.
Approval of the August 8 special town election warrant was put off a week so town counsel can review new mailing-notice language.
The board also adopted the current IRS mileage rate, named a new detective and other appointees, and reviewed executive-session employment agreements for several town staff.

why_it_matters: A stalled union contract leaves DPW workers' pay and terms unresolved and keeps a labor cost decision open for the town.
The eminent domain action affects a specific property owner on Flatill Road and clears the way for a town bridge project residents depend on.
The election warrant delay and the mailing-notice review could affect how voters are notified ahead of the August 8 special town election.

meetings.headline: The committee voted unanimously to ask the select board for a special town meeting to redirect state aid into the school budget.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard extensive public comment on middle school athletics funding, booster fundraising, and academic performance following the failed override, then reviewed routine business (minutes, a donation, four line-item transfers, warrants, and encumbrances). The superintendent reported on transportation vans, a facilities earmark, staffing changes, and Title IX/booster-donation guidance; the committee also approved an adult meal price increase, relocated the T-ball program to accommodate the food pantry, accepted a curriculum report describing the loss of all reading interventionists and larger class sizes, accepted a strong FY26 quarterly budget report, accepted a personnel report with numerous departures attributed to budget uncertainty, and voted unanimously to ask the select board to convene a special town meeting to direct additional state chapter 70 and other cherry sheet funds into the school budget.

public_comment.topic: Argues the override failed due to lost public confidence, not messaging; cites accreditation risk and reading proficiency, urges review of support programs, academic prioritization, IEP audit, and accountability.

public_comment.speaker_as_heard: Matt Nzareno (heard also as Matt Ezaro)
public_comment.topic: Presented a by-sport athletics cost/revenue analysis built from FY24 actuals, arguing middle school sports were revenue-positive and questioning the decision to cut them for budget reasons.
Spoke on behalf of the community about restoring middle school athletics, requesting a detailed cost/revenue breakdown by sport and guidance on applying community-raised funds, by mid-July.

Requested permission to purchase five football helmets and to fund one-way transportation to away games using booster funds, and pushed back on the characterization of football boosters as "wealthier" than other programs.

meetings.summary: The Lunenburg Select Board ratified two seasonal appointments, adopted an updated environmentally preferable purchasing policy, and voted to support a legislative letter urging retention of the Foundation Budget Review Commission and higher school aid levels in the FY27 state budget. The town manager reported progress on a temporary food pantry site at the former School Street school, the awarded Flat Hill Road Bridge contract, and a dangerous/nuisance dog complaint headed to a standalone hearing; the board also scheduled a July 14 goals workshop, approved several sets of prior minutes, heard numerous committee reports, and voted to enter executive session on non-union personnel matters.

meetings.headline: The Select Board reconstituted the Personnel Committee as a five-member body and filled its seats along with most other town board vacancies.
meetings.summary: This Select Board meeting was devoted entirely to annual appointments and reappointments to town boards, committees and commissions, with the board interviewing each applicant briefly before voting. By the end of the meeting the board had filled seats on the APDC, Council on Aging, Americans with Disabilities Committee, Conservation Committee, Cultural Council, Green Communities and a newly reconstituted five-member Personnel Committee, leaving remaining vacancies only on Conservation, Cultural Council, Historical Commission and PAC.

The board noted the Americans with Disabilities Committee likely cannot meet again until it has a member-at-large and a select board representative assigned, which may not happen until August.

meetings.headline: Committee debated reopening FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but leaned toward not disturbing the town-meeting-approved budget
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee spent most of the meeting debating whether newly-added state Senate aid should prompt reconsideration of the FY27 budget just approved at town meeting, with members split between honoring the town-meeting result and revisiting free cash, reserve, and OPEB policies given the tight fiscal situation. No formal budget action was taken; the only votes were procedural approval of past minutes and adjournment, while the committee set its next meeting for June 11th and agreed to revisit financial policy work and the tri-board process ahead of FY28.

public_comment.topic: Asked for feedback during the meeting rather than only at the end; raised concern about a select board member's resignation, whether the roughly $400,000/$465,000 in added state aid is directed to Lunenburg, distress over reading program shortfalls in the lower grades, and the cost of PFAS-contaminated fire department turnout gear.
Reminder of the June 3rd water district election and a Sunday town fair event, plus thanks to outgoing member Jean.

A member said the state Senate has increased aid to Lunenburg in various lines, money she believes could eventually land in free cash rather than be appropriated to the schools now facing cuts.

budget_items.topic: Finance committee reserve account vs. financial policy minimum
budget_items.what_was_said: A member contrasted how the finance committee reserve account was funded against the financial policy's stated minimum, arguing the town manager could be asked to look at using added state aid to help the school budget.

budget_items.topic: Using added state revenue at a special town meeting
budget_items.what_was_said: The chair noted that if additional state aid is finalized, the town would not spend it all at once and could adjust the budget allocation at a special town meeting.
A member noted that a sum the senator secured for Lunenburg last year likely ended up as part of the free cash built up through conservative budgeting.
The chair said current policy sets a $50k minimum reserve but allows up to roughly a 0.5% cap, giving flexibility for tight-budget years.

A resident asked whether a large sum moving through the state Senate has been specifically directed to Lunenburg; the chair said it is still working through reconciliation and has not been signed into law.
A resident described the cost of replacing PFAS-contaminated firefighter turnout gear as a large, currently unaddressed capital-type need, having discussed it with the fire chief months earlier.

Local receipts have not come in below a certain level for the past decade; this year's estimate was set lower and then adjusted upward slightly by the town manager. A member argued for reconsidering how conservatively local receipts are projected given the current budget strain.
A member asked how much free cash the town has this year and historically; the chair gave a rough figure and acknowledged not having the full ten-year history on hand.
The town currently puts a set percentage into OPEB annually per policy; a member questioned whether that approach should be revisited given current budget pressure.
A resident said he was told banks and bonding companies expect continued OPEB-type contributions, citing a large unaddressed liability, and argued token contributions would not be adequate.
The school committee is expected to bring forward a plan for Turkey Hill that will involve a major rebuild or rehabilitation; the town is currently well positioned financially to handle it.

A resident raised concern about reported structural issues with the school bleachers area, which a member confirmed has been discussed at the capital planning committee as an item exceeding normal capital thresholds.

meetings.headline: Override failed; committee accepts a balanced-budget of cuts and eyes another override attempt next year
meetings.summary: The committee processed the fallout of the failed override, with the superintendent outlining the resulting cuts (class sizes, interventionists, middle school sports and transportation, high school world language) and recommending the district implement the balanced budget and form a community task force rather than return to voters immediately. The committee elected new officers for 2026-2027 -- Laura as chair, Tony as vice chair, Mandy Gilman provisionally as secretary -- adopted several revised policies (cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, advertising), tabled the fifth-grade bus-release procedure pending community feedback, and voted a composite evaluation of the superintendent's first year.

what_happened.line: After the override failed, the committee leaned toward implementing a balanced budget built on cuts to class sizes, interventionists, middle school sports and transportation, and high school world language, rather than returning to voters right away.
The committee elected Laura as chair and Tony as vice chair for 2026-2027, with Mandy Gilman named secretary pending her acceptance.

The committee adopted revised policies on cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, and advertising in schools.
The committee accepted a composite evaluation of the superintendent's first year.

why_it_matters: The override's failure is now translating into specific reductions -- class sizes, interventionist staffing, middle school sports and transportation, and a high school language program -- while the committee weighs a community task force before deciding whether to ask voters again.
The new cash-handling policy sets a cap on cash accepted per school transaction, which came up directly in connection with how prom tickets can be sold going forward.

Families with fourth- and fifth-graders should watch for the superintendent's community feedback process on bus release, since it is being handled as an administrative procedure rather than a committee policy vote.

meetings.headline: Select Board held final public comment on the override before Saturday's town election; the chair backed a yes vote.
meetings.summary: The Select Board held its final public comment session before Saturday's annual town election and Proposition 2½ override vote, hearing residents both for and against the override, then the chair publicly stated support for the override. The board also ratified a police executive assistant hire, approved two youth achievement proclamations, assigned a police officer (not the elected constable) to cover the election, approved an FY27 state advocacy letter on school funding, voted to sell two tax-title Hollis Road parcels, and entered executive session at the close.

budget_items.what_was_said: A resident argued the town's roughly $1.4 million in new growth revenue was split unevenly, with capital projects, a finance committee reserve above policy, and a new town manager hire funded while schools were left short of level-service funding.
A resident said the added annual tax bill under the override was unreasonable given current gas prices, citing figures for homes in a stated value range.
The board was asked to approve appointing Kimberly Murphy at a specific wage step in addition to ratifying her hire.
The board's advocacy letter urges the senator to increase circuit breaker funding to a stated reimbursement percentage under a specific line item.

budget_items.topic: Section 3 local aid for minimum aid districts
budget_items.what_was_said: The letter urges a minimum per-pupil local aid distribution for minimum aid districts like Lunenburg.
The letter thanks the senator for a proposed increase to statewide UGGA funding, citing the increase and resulting total.

budget_items.topic: Sale of tax-title property, 250 and 356 Hollis Road
budget_items.what_was_said: The board discussed disposing of two tax-title parcels after other town boards had recommended selling; no dollar figures were stated.

decisions.decision: Board members informally agreed to default to police coverage rather than the elected constable for the annual town election, citing concerns about the constable's public statements on the override, ahead of the formal vote.
Board agreed to add the school committee and finance committee as CC recipients on the FY27 advocacy letter to Senator Cronin before signing.
Board agreed to aim to complete the town manager's annual evaluation the week following the town election, once outstanding board member input is compiled.

The most substantive content was extended public comment in which a resident challenged claims that the FY27 balanced budget and override option cut fire and police services, followed by another resident promoting property-tax relief programs; the meeting closed by voting to enter executive session over firefighter and AFSCME collective bargaining strategy.

budget_items.topic: Fire department Sunday shift staffing cost, PDM coverage vs. career firefighters
budget_items.what_was_said: A public commenter said last year she pointed out the cost difference between PDM ambulance coverage and hiring career firefighters for the Sunday shift. She suggested the Sunday shift could again be added without an override, as is being done this year.

budget_items.topic: FY26 school department level-services budget request
budget_items.what_was_said: A commenter recalled the school department requesting an increase for level services in the FY26 process and said she raised concerns the numbers did not align.

budget_items.topic: FY25 override funds left unspent by the school department
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said a portion of the FY25 override went unspent due to lack of tracking under the former superintendent, which she said hurt students.

budget_items.topic: New assistant town hall manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said the town manager's balanced budget adds a new assistant town hall manager position at an added cost, while eliminating one existing position.

budget_items.topic: Town reserve account vs. financial policy threshold
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said the balanced budget sets aside a reserve amount well above what the town's financial policy calls for.

budget_items.topic: New revenue used for capital expenses including vehicles
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter said new revenue is being used for capital expenses including vehicles rather than drawing from an existing reserve account.
The commenter listed the band concert as a small service being eliminated in the balanced budget.
The commenter cited the town beach's net cost as another small service affected by budget choices.
The commenter framed the eliminated small services as insignificant relative to the total town budget, but said they matter to affected families and seniors.

budget_items.topic: School reserve accounts vs. amount needed for current services
budget_items.what_was_said: The commenter questioned why school reserve accounts exceed what she said is needed to maintain current services, given warnings that schools would be devastated if the override fails.

budget_items.topic: 41A property tax deferral and circuit breaker eligibility thresholds
budget_items.what_was_said: A resident described income and home-value thresholds under the state's 41A deferral and circuit breaker tax credit programs, saying eligibility is broader than residents realize.

budget_items.topic: State income tax circuit breaker credit
budget_items.what_was_said: The same resident said qualifying residents could also get an income tax break under the circuit breaker program.

budget_items.topic: Means-tested tax relief program income and asset limits
budget_items.what_was_said: The resident described household income and asset limits for a means-tested relief program, encouraging seniors to check eligibility with the assessors.

decisions.decision: Board held off formally appointing the AFSCME/SAP representative to the sick leave bank committee, since it was not specifically posted on this agenda; to be brought back on a future agenda.
Board agreed to hold the vote on 250 and 356 Hollis Road open until May 12th to allow time for input from planning, agricultural, open space/conservation, and assessors.
Board agreed the Hollis Road referral to those boards/committees can go out now rather than waiting for a future meeting.
Board agreed to wait until after annual town meeting before resuming work on the special event policy.
Board agreed members need more time to review the updated employee climate survey questions before approving them, aiming to issue the survey sometime in May.
Board agreed to ask town counsel (Adam) whether the FY27 budget/override open house needs to be posted as an open meeting given a possible quorum of members attending.

meetings.headline: Schools urged town unity ahead of the override vote; routine grants and policy readings were approved
meetings.summary: The meeting was dominated by the superintendent and chair urging the town to approach the upcoming Proposition 2½ override and town meeting collaboratively rather than divisively, describing this year's tri-board budget process as unusually transparent. The committee also heard a LEAF Foundation fundraising update, approved two state grant submissions and a farm-to-school grant, discussed a scholarship trust/EIN dispute with the town's Trust Commission, revisited unified sports options, reviewed the quarterly budget and personnel reports, assigned negotiating teams for two union contracts, set a process for the superintendent's evaluation, and waived first readings on four policies.

Neither record is treated as the referee.

meetings.headline: Public comment turned into a pitched fight over the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and a disputed Ledger story.
meetings.summary: The bulk of this meeting was public comment: the fire chief, both police and fire union presidents, a school committee member speaking as a parent, and residents disputed a local newspaper's coverage of the FY27 balanced budget, override, and staffing cuts, followed by lengthy rebuttals from board members and the Town Manager. The board also handled routine license and event-permit hearings, a town manager's report, tax-title property and cover-photo votes, committee reports, and voted to enter executive session over opioid-litigation settlement strategy; no vote was taken on the override itself.

public_comment.stated_role: former Board of Assessors member, resident
public_comment.topic: Reminds the public that the 41A senior tax deferral program still exists though it is not well publicized, relevant to concerns about affording taxes if an override passes.

public_comment.stated_role: president of the Lunenburg Professional Firefighters Local 5369
public_comment.topic: Defends the fire department's fourth-shift proposal and ambulance staffing, disputes comparisons made to another town's fire department.

public_comment.stated_role: resident, co-author of Lunenburg Ledger budget articles
public_comment.topic: Presents findings from a series of Ledger articles on budget cost drivers, argues the town and schools need more money and supports the override.

public_comment.stated_role: resident, parent, voter (not speaking as a School Committee member)
public_comment.topic: Argues the balanced budget's cuts disproportionately affect children and youth services and urges the board to weigh children's needs as constituents.
Announces an upcoming trivia fundraiser, memorializes a late community member, and offers advisory remarks urging voters not to view the override debate as driven by bad intent.

minutes.headline: Public comment turned into a pitched fight over the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and a disputed Ledger story.
minutes.summary: The bulk of this meeting was public comment: the fire chief, both police and fire union presidents, a school committee member speaking as a parent, and residents disputed a local newspaper's coverage of the FY27 balanced budget, override, and staffing cuts, followed by lengthy rebuttals from board members and the Town Manager. The board also handled routine license and event-permit hearings, a town manager's report, tax-title property and cover-photo votes, committee reports, and voted to enter executive session over opioid-litigation settlement strategy; no vote was taken on the override itself.

what_happened.line: Public comment and board rebuttals covered the FY27 override, staffing cuts, and disputed newspaper coverage, but no vote was taken on the override.
The fire chief and firefighters' union president defended a proposed fourth fire shift, saying the staffing plan has not changed since last July.
The police union president disputed characterizations of town free cash as an available surplus, calling it one-time money for capital needs.
The Town Manager publicly rebutted a newspaper's article point by point on free cash, the deficit, and other disputed claims.
The board tabled a decision on selling two tax-title Hollis Road parcels until members can visit the properties.

why_it_matters: The dispute over budget figures and staffing plans bears directly on how residents weigh the FY27 override at town meeting.
Fire and police staffing levels discussed here affect emergency response coverage funded by the override.
Whether the town sells or keeps the Hollis Road parcels affects future town land use and potential revenue.

minutes.summary: The Select Board finalized its annual town meeting warrant, voting to recommend approval of the FY27 balanced budget, both tiers of the proposed override, and several enterprise fund articles, after lengthy public comment and board debate over cuts to services versus a new assistant town manager position and fourth fire shift. The board also approved the election warrant, appointed a new APDC member, sent a letter opposing state legislation on excise-tax enforcement, and set a budget public information meeting before entering executive session on DPW union negotiations.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to recommend the FY27 balanced budget for town meeting.
The board recommended the override's second tier by a 3-1 vote; the first tier's vote outcome was not audible on the recording.
Public commenters objected to proposed cuts to the library, senior center and beach program alongside new spending on an assistant town manager and a fourth fire shift.
The board also recommended the PAC/PEG, solid waste, water and sewer enterprise fund articles, all unanimously.
The board scheduled a budget public information meeting for the evening of April 28 at the Adult Activity Center.

why_it_matters: Both the balanced budget and the override now go to town meeting, where the choice is between a level-services budget with cuts to programs like the library, senior center and beach program, or an override that funds the assistant town manager position and a fourth fire shift.
A resident weighing the override should note the split board vote on its second tier, which signals the choice was not unanimous even among the officials recommending it.
The April 28 public information meeting is the town's forum for residents to ask about the budget and override before voting.

Two override tiers would go to voters as separate ballot questions, with only the highest approved amount implemented; the Finance Committee deferred taking a position pending the full board.

An accounting error had moved the same unspent FY23 capital funds through two prior votes (TCP roof repair, then FY26 capital); this article unwinds both so the money returns to the FY26 capital plan cleanly.

Individual capital items were read out including DPW bridge completion, a police cruiser, a fire engine/brush truck, primary school entry/driveway and playground design, public safety building roof and boiler work, door security intercoms at Turkey Hill and the primary school, and a DPW front-end loader.
The planned motion would transfer this amount from solid waste enterprise revenue to operate the program for FY2027; the fund does not cover recycling costs.
The fund would use enterprise revenue to pay Fitchburg for water and recoup a percentage under an intermunicipal agreement; figures were based on usage estimates.
A transfer toward the sewer enterprise's share of retiree health benefit liability; a member asked why the PEG/PAC enterprise carries no similar contribution.
Total FY2027 operating budget figure for the sewer enterprise fund.

budget_items.topic: SAP salary schedule / cost of living adjustment
budget_items.what_was_said: A cost-of-living increase for non-union salaried employees would be funded from the salary reserve; a member clarified it is not tied to any federal COLA figure.

budget_items.topic: Special appropriation: TC Pasio and assessor position
budget_items.what_was_said: Funds requested for TC Pasio operating and decommissioning costs and for a special assistant to the assessor position.

budget_items.topic: Free cash to OPEB trust fund
budget_items.what_was_said: Ten percent of certified free cash was described as being transferred to the OPEB trust under the town's financial policy.
A second consecutive year of a small deposit was proposed to build a cushion against retirement buyout costs exceeding the operating budget line.
Funds requested for activities marking the town's 300th anniversary; some members felt the amount was too large given past reliance on volunteers.
A standard annual transfer from free cash to the general-purpose stabilization fund, distinct from the vehicle/special purpose fund.

A new deposit was proposed as a cushion against a future spike in health insurance costs; total town and school insurance costs across active and retiree accounts were estimated. One member asked for defined trigger criteria for using the fund before supporting it.

budget_items.topic: Vacation accrual system transition liability buyout
budget_items.what_was_said: The town proposed buying out the full accrued-vacation liability at current dollar value ahead of a transition to a continuous accrual system, covering SAP employees and settled/near-settled union groups.
A member recalled roughly this figure as the cost of printing and mailing full warrant booklets to every household, cited in favor of switching to a postcard notice.

reconciliation.what: Our minutes against the minutes the town published. caption_error = the same fact the captions rendered badly, resolved by the official reading shown beside the as-heard one; discrepancy = a substantive difference, flagged and not resolved. Neither record is treated as the referee.
reconciliation.summary: The two records agree closely on the mechanics of nearly every vote (motion, outcome, and any split count) once articles are matched up, but they diverge in two ways worth flagging: the official minutes record every dollar figure zero times (they give motion/seconder/roll-call only), so almost none of "ours" many dollar amounts can be checked against them, and there are several real vote-outcome conflicts — Article Q (300th anniversary) is unanimous in the official record but "4-1" in ours, Article P (compensated absence reserve) has a Jay Simeone nay the official record shows but ours omits, and two articles ours marked "not audible" (O, Z2) the official record shows were unanimously approved. A reader should check the actual warrant to resolve which SAP article (N vs. EE) corresponds to the "Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade" item ours describes, since the two records' SAP-related outcomes don't cleanly line up.

what_happened.line: The committee put off recommending a position on the FY27 Proposition 2½ override until the full five-member board can meet.
It also deferred the FY27 omnibus town and school operating budget because final transfer figures were not yet ready.
A new special-purpose health insurance stabilization fund transfer passed its recommendation on a 4-1 vote.
A proposed Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade change was pushed to the next meeting after members said it needed further discussion.
Most routine warrant articles -- revolving funds, the FY27 capital budget, and the water and solid waste enterprise funds -- were recommended for approval.

why_it_matters: The override recommendation touches what residents are asked to approve at town meeting or the ballot, and the committee is not yet on record with a position.
The FY27 omnibus budget funds town and school operations for the coming year; its numbers were not final at this meeting.
The health insurance stabilization fund is a new savings mechanism for a cost that affects both town and school budgets, and it did not pass without dissent.
watch_next: The next Finance Committee meeting, when the full board is expected to take up the override recommendation.
A future vote on the FY27 omnibus town/school budget article, once closeout and transfer figures are final.

meetings.headline: Committee voted to keep charging the student bus fee despite members calling it unfair, citing budget desperation.
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee heard public comment on an override, a student proposal to credit after-school sports as PE, and updates on capital projects and grant-seeking, then worked through a long list of votes: continuing the bus fee, discontinuing the lifelong learning program, approving a $300,000 federal earmark request, and endorsing a letter to legislators on Chapter 70 funding. Facilities updates covered an energy-efficiency program at the high school, relocating a generator from the Pacios building, solar array repairs, and Turkey Hill bathroom renovations, alongside several retirement and new-hire announcements including a new Turkey Hill principal.

public_comment.topic: Advocated that participation in after-school sports count as PE/gym credit for high schoolers, citing a student survey and studies on mental health benefits.
Raised concerns about the override not being a permanent fix, wanted long-range financial projections, and described rising need at the local food pantry and community mutual aid.
Reminded residents that the override must pass at both the May 2nd town meeting and the May 16th ballot, and urged attendance at both.
Raised concern that unified sports/arts opportunities for students with disabilities are shrinking and asked for a fuller committee conversation on options.

budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager approved three capital requests: two feasibility studies for the primary school (playground and drive/playground) and camera systems for building entrances. Other requested items were deferred for later in the year due to funding and the Pacios building situation.

The district is seeking one-time federal earmark funding to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset a projected cut to Title One funding; the district would not have to make up any shortfall if the full amount isn't awarded.
Funds previously voted to be accepted from the scholarship fund were not actually transferred from the estate to students due to a legal/executor issue; the district will bring it back once resolved.
As of month-end the district was at 66.1% of budget expended, rising to 68.6% once a payroll posted; last year the district was at 67% at the same point, having spent less overall.
The collaborative tuition line is overspent because circuit breaker reimbursement money has not yet been posted back into it; this is described as a normally hard line to budget.

Electrical spending is running over budget due to a colder winter and last year's underbudgeting; gas/heating has money remaining, and next year's electrical budget was adjusted based on recent actuals.
Legal expenses are running hot this year and the FY27 budget has been adjusted upward as a result.

The district described fee revenue collected over two periods and the fee schedule by family size and reduced-fee eligibility, and members debated the fairness of the fee against the roughly $70,000 it raises given the district's financial situation.

Chapter 70 does not include transportation costs at all, and regional districts get 75% of transportation reimbursed while Lunenburg does not, which a member said could be worth a large additional sum if reimbursed similarly.

The adult men's basketball program generated minimal revenue per player and relies on unpaid volunteer facilitators; the adult health and fitness program is a pass-through to a private vendor with the district retaining no financial benefit, supporting the recommendation to discontinue the district-run program.

A draft letter to legislators notes Lunenburg ranks near the bottom statewide for per-pupil spending while spending well above the state-required minimum, which members attribute to flaws in how Chapter 70 categorizes districts.
A building-controls efficiency study at the high school may be covered up to 100% by the program, addressing malfunctioning thermostats and actuators causing temperature problems.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to continue charging the student bus fee for another year, despite members calling it unfair, citing the district's financial situation.
Members voted to end the district-run Lunenburg lifelong learning program effective June 1, citing minimal revenue and reliance on volunteers or a pass-through vendor.
The committee authorized the superintendent to pursue a one-time federal earmark to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset an expected cut to Title One funding.
Members endorsed a letter to state legislators arguing Lunenburg's Chapter 70 funding formula undercounts its per-pupil spending and excludes transportation costs.
The FY26 monthly budget report showed spending running ahead of the same point last year, with the electrical and legal lines over budget.

why_it_matters: The bus fee stays in place for families who use it, separate from and regardless of the outcome of the townwide override vote in May.
Ending the lifelong learning program removes a district-run adult offering, though students already enrolled will finish the current session before it closes.
The letter to legislators is an ask, not a change in funding -- any shift in how Chapter 70 treats transportation or per-pupil spending depends on action in Boston, not this committee.

meetings.headline: Board set the FY27 town meeting warrant and voted a two-tier override question onto the town election ballot
meetings.summary: The Select Board worked through the annual town meeting warrant article by article with town counsel, deferring several items (prior-year invoices, FY26 budget adjustments, the snow-and-ice closeout, and union contract funding) to town meeting itself, and declining -- after individual members stated concerns -- to include a Trust Fund Commission legal-fees article or a quorum bylaw article that counsel flagged as legally uncertain. The board voted to place a two-tier Proposition 2½ override question on the annual town election ballot, rounding the tiers to clean dollar figures and choosing a "Question 1/Question 2" ballot format, while one member stated ongoing concerns about the override's affordability. It also discussed but did not finalize where the override and other articles should sit in the warrant order and consent agenda.

No votes were taken on the budget, override, or warrant articles at this meeting; the committee closed the public hearing, reviewed draft warrant articles, and scheduled an additional virtual meeting for April 6th to vote on articles and finalize its report before the town meeting warrant deadline.

meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to finalize the structure and dollar figures of a Proposition 2½ override for the May town meeting and ballot, after months of separate budget work. They voted to pursue a two-tier override rather than one number, agreed to pull a stormwater utility request out of the override for now, and the School Committee raised its lower-tier ask to 1.6 million; officials could not guarantee the higher tier would prevent another override request next year, and the boards turned to planning joint public messaging before adjourning.

Praises the transparency of this budget season; urges putting storm water back into the budget rather than removing it, and recommends the town buy a GIS subscription so it stops paying consultants to remake the same maps.

Questions whether even the highest override tier truly buys two years of level service, warns fear-based messaging has an expiration date, and again urges a multi-year projection and cost-per-home examples for the messaging campaign.

what_happened.line: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee voted unanimously to pursue a two-tier FY27 override rather than a single override number.
The boards pulled stormwater out of the tier-two override and chose not to bring a standalone stormwater override article this cycle, deferring to the stormwater task force.

meetings.headline: Committee picked one override number (core "Scenario C") and, if it fails, will cut athletic transportation to save a teacher and a therapy aide
meetings.summary: The School Committee spent most of a long meeting building two FY27 budgets: an override ask (core "scenario C," roughly $1.5-1.6 million) that it voted to send to the Select Board as a single number, and a "balanced" no-override budget that cuts classroom teachers, an assistant principal, a custodian, an occupational therapy assistant, and other positions through attrition. After extended debate over cutting athletics versus classroom staff, the committee voted to accept the balanced budget minus the athletic transportation line, directing the superintendent's team to decide how to reallocate that cut to restore a teacher and an occupational therapy assistant. Members also voted to formalize the town's PEC health-insurance opt-out enhancement, approved a scholarship payout, an international trip, and childcare-program handbook changes.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to send the Select Board one override number, built from a "core" budget option, instead of asking for two tiers.

It also voted to accept a no-override "balanced" budget but cut athletic transportation instead of a teacher, and told staff to find a way to restore that teacher and an occupational therapy aide position.
Members added back a small music-teacher position to the override budget to preserve fifth-grade band.
The committee voted to move forward on a richer health-insurance opt-out incentive for employees who decline coverage.
A resident in public comment asked, without answer in the minutes, what happened to money left over from a prior override.

why_it_matters: Town meeting voters will be asked to approve a single override figure built from this "core" budget, so this is the number that reaches the ballot.

If the override fails, whether a classroom teacher and an occupational therapy aide keep their positions now depends on how the district reallocates the athletic-transportation cut, a decision still pending from the superintendent's team.
The health-insurance opt-out change affects what the town and school pay employees who decline coverage, on both the town and school side of the budget.

meetings.headline: Finance Committee reviewed FY27 department budgets amid a large town-school funding gap, with an override now expected.
meetings.summary: The Finance Committee heard FY27 budget presentations from DPW/sewer, land use, and general government departments, plus a trust fund commissioners' warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds, which the committee suggested moving to a special town meeting for a firmer estimate. No budget votes were taken; the committee recapped a prior tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, split on whether it should be one or two amounts, and rescheduled its public hearing and a tri-board meeting for the following weeks.

attendees.role: director of planning and economic development

public_comment.topic: Reported that the earlier audio problem hearing remote Zoom participants was a setting on the Zoom back end, not the meeting's own equipment.

votes.motion: Motion to adjourn.

budget_items.what_was_said: The general fund free cash was certified this week; Karen Brochu was thanked for putting together the free cash submission to the state.
Bill Bernard presented an overall DPW budget higher than previous years, covering mandatory work, a new part-time clerk, restored pavement management, and MS4 storm water compliance money.

Bernard's budget restores pavement management to $650,000 'where it should be,' while the town manager's preliminary budget shows only $279,000; a committee member said they will not support the restoration in the final budget.
Street light electricity costs were estimated at $30,000 originally, came in just over $30,500, then rose further; the line moved into DPW's budget after conversion to LED lighting.
Bernard requested a $340,000 increase in the storm water line item to get closer to MS4 permit compliance, covering catch basin cleaning and street sweeping.

budget_items.topic: Catch basin cleaning and sweeping performance
budget_items.what_was_said: In-house work over the last three years has completed about 30% of catch basin cleaning and 22% of street sweeping, well short of what is mandated.
Bernard estimated it would cost about $100,000 less per year to contract out catch basin cleaning and sweeping than to hire three additional staff.
Bernard modeled a 3% annual increase for DPW, clerical union, and himself across FY25-27 to estimate roughly $52,000 in added salary cost, pending ongoing CBA negotiations.
The snow and ice budget is being increased 2.5% per year to close the gap between budget and actual spending, currently around $800,000.
Vehicle repair costs sent out to contractors exceeded the budgeted line significantly last year, prompting a requested increase.
The recycling budget was reduced after a closer look at actual spending; last year's budget was much higher than what is actually being spent.
The trash program is described as roughly self-funding at about $500,000 per year.
DPW cited a small bridge grant for the Flaill road bridge, a storm water asset management grant from the Mass Clean Water Trust, and a pending Mass Community Cover grant for engineering on a culvert.
Bernard plans to apply for a Complete Streets grant and has a cost estimate of about a million dollars for sidewalk construction and repair between the high school and Marshall Park.
Chapter 90 funding for FY27 is expected at a higher level than the typical amount; continuing at the higher level over several years would add nearly $1.7 million versus normal funding.
The sewer enterprise fund budget is just under $2 million, with expenses and revenues nearly balanced showing an estimated small surplus.
The town pays Leominster and Fitchburg to treat sewage since Lunenburg has no treatment plant of its own; this is the largest driver of the sewer budget.
The engineering line was budgeted at $30,000 last year but actual cost was $80,000 after DEP required additional engineering work; the line is being increased again.
Money is set aside to replace aging pumps, controllers, and pipe as the sewer system approaches the end of its design life.

Without a rate increase, user charge revenue was estimated to leave a large deficit; with the proposed rate increase the budget shows only a small surplus, avoiding further draws on retained earnings.
The proposed sewer rate increase is about 16%, driven by Leominster and Fitchburg raising their own disposal charges.

The per-unit user rate would rise from its current level to a higher figure (about 16% increase), while the minimum charge rises only about 5%, intended to soften the impact on lower-usage households.

budget_items.topic: Sewer grant indirect cost line (health insurance)
budget_items.what_was_said: This line, which covers the sewer enterprise's share of health insurance and treasurer/collector office costs, was questioned for how it compares to prior years' actuals and budgets amid an 8% health insurance increase.
Total sewer expenses were compared across FY25 actual, FY26 budget, and FY27 request.
The combined conservation, building, and planning/economic development budget request represents a modest increase, driven mainly by step and cost-of-living increases.

budget_items.topic: Land use mapping purchase of services line
budget_items.what_was_said: A new line item funds mapping for zoning changes and proposals that previously had no dedicated funding mechanism.
About 16% of land use funding comes from the general fund, roughly 75% from building permit fees, and about 4% from specialty permits.
Some shovel-ready projects have not yet pulled permits; the building department has roughly this much in expected but uncollected permit fee receivables.

budget_items.topic: Trust funds legal investigation warrant article
budget_items.what_was_said: The trust fund commissioners requested this appropriation to fund roughly 40 hours of professional legal investigation into several long-neglected municipal trust funds.
The requested amount was calculated as approximately 40 hours of investigation at $350 per hour, covering all five flagged trust funds.

budget_items.topic: Total trust fund dollars at stake
budget_items.what_was_said: John Bowen said the funds under dispute total in this range, currently unable to be distributed to Lunenburg residents and veterans without a legal investigation.

budget_items.topic: Nathaniel Day worthy poor fund original gift
budget_items.what_was_said: The 1901 donation establishing the worthy poor fund is estimated to be worth this much in today's dollars.
The town manager cited the school budget figure under full restoration as part of the overall FY27 budget update.
The presenter stated an overall projected budget deficit split between town and school portions.

budget_items.topic: Property tax levy and revenue estimates
budget_items.what_was_said: Property tax levy and total revenue estimates were cited, along with adjustments to motor vehicle excise and investment income revenue lines.
The overall general government budget changed slightly from the preliminary figure to the current figure presented tonight.

budget_items.topic: Town manager's office budget / assistant town manager position
budget_items.what_was_said: The town manager's budget rose substantially to fund a new assistant town manager position for a full year; restructuring by eliminating the communications/IT director position reduced the net new cost from $120,000 to $60,000.
Audit costs are rising because the town's former auditing firm was absorbed into a larger firm (CBIZ) at greater cost, and a competing firm lacked capacity to take on the town.
Small reductions were made to the treasurer and collector office budgets based on actual spending, including contracted services covering the deputy tax collector and Unibank services.
The assessor's budget is nearly level; a temporary special assistant position is being moved out of the operating budget to one-time funding; abatement counts have declined from a 2023 spike.
FY26 and FY25 real estate exemption counts and total dollar amounts were compared; the senior means-tested exemption was not approved for FY2025.
The town clerk's overall budget is roughly level, but the elections line rises sharply because 2026 is an election year with a September primary and November general election.
The APDC physicals budget was increased due to under-budgeting, and a new economic development committee line funds an annual town official meet-and-greet event.
The town report/printing line rose sharply because it had not been properly budgeted, covering the annual report, town meeting booklet, and special town meeting warrant printing and mailing.
The reserve fund is level funded; the town manager raised the idea of increasing it given department budgets are being tightened, citing prior years' transfer amounts.
The salary reserve has not been adjusted for FY27 pending outcomes of ongoing DPW, clerical, and firefighter contract negotiations; an anticipated 3% COLA for non-union (SAP) employees is assumed.
Central purchasing, which now includes consolidated postage costs, is level funded.
The veterans budget is largely driven by Chapter 115 benefit payments currently serving seven residents; the town receives trailing state reimbursement the following fiscal year.
This line rose almost entirely due to the non-discretionary Worcester County retirement assessment.
The unclassified budget, covering liability, workers comp, health, life insurance, unemployment and Medicare, increased from the preliminary figure due to a correction in Medicare supplement counts.
Liability insurance covers property/casualty with a rate guarantee through FY27, plus a separate injured-on-duty policy for police and fire and a small risk-management training line.
Workers compensation was reduced based on conversations with the town's insurance representative, applying available credits.
Group health insurance, the largest piece of the unclassified budget, increased; a separate line funds employees who opt out of coverage.
Retiree health insurance covers town and school retirees at estimated Medicare Blue and Medex rates, plus a Medicare supplement paid twice yearly.

what_happened.line: Finance Committee recapped a tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, but remained split on whether it should be one amount or two.

DPW's proposed FY27 budget came in higher than prior years, restoring pavement management funding the town manager's preliminary budget had cut, though one committee member said they will not support that restoration.
The town manager's office is being restructured: the communications and IT director position would be eliminated and a new assistant town manager position funded starting July 1.

The committee recommended moving a warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds from the annual town meeting to a special town meeting, so a firmer cost estimate can be developed first.
The FY27 budget public hearing was pushed back one week to March 26, with a tri-board meeting taking the committee's March 19 slot instead.

why_it_matters: An override, once the ballot format is settled, would raise property taxes for residents and the one-question-versus-two split changes how they vote on it.
The DPW budget still has to be finalized, and whether pavement management funding is restored affects road paving work and how storm water permit compliance gets funded.
The town manager's office restructuring changes which staff position handles human resources and IT/communications duties going forward.
watch_next: The rescheduled FY27 budget public hearing on March 26
The tri-board meeting on March 19 to resolve the one-override-vs-two-override question

meetings.headline: TriBoard split near evenly on one FY27 override vs. two tiers, but agreed unanimously to put one on the ballot.
meetings.summary: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee met jointly to debate how to structure a Proposition 2½ override for next year's budget, weighing a single combined ask against tiered options. Every member present favored putting some override on the ballot, but the group was closely divided over one number versus two, and no final figure was set that night. Town Counsel joined by phone to explain ballot procedure and campaign-finance limits, and the boards deferred a joint public statement, aiming to settle on a number in the coming weeks.

what_happened.line: The three boards voted unanimously to place a Proposition 2½ override question on the ballot, with no final amount set that night.
A straw poll on a single combined override versus two tiered options came out closely split, with the count itself unclear in the recording and several members absent.
Rather than issue a joint statement on the straw poll, each board agreed to share updates through its own channels, since the Select Board had not yet finished its own line-by-line budget review.
The boards set a goal of agreeing on an override number by late March or early April, ahead of the deadline to hand ballot language to the town clerk.
The School Committee will present its balanced, cuts-based budget at its March 18 meeting.

why_it_matters: Whatever number the boards settle on becomes the property tax increase every household is asked to approve at town meeting.

A single override versus a tiered one changes what is guaranteed to residents versus what depends on a second vote later — school staff positions were named specifically as at stake in either version.
The March 18 School Committee presentation of the cuts budget is the baseline every override option is being measured against.

what_happened.line: The committee voted to send the finance committee an FY27 budget it says the town cannot fund without an override.
Members said they favor one unified, townwide override rather than separate amounts by school or grade.
The committee will not detail what gets cut to balance the budget without an override until its March 18 meeting.
The committee also approved several grant proposals, capped virtual-school enrollment, and adopted the FY26-27 school calendar.
A speaker during public comment urged the committee to hold off alarming the public until the actual funding need is known.

why_it_matters: This budget is described as restoring positions cut the prior year, and the committee says funding it depends on an override, a vote that would raise property taxes beyond the normal cap.

The grant, enrollment-cap and calendar votes are procedural and do not depend on the override outcome.

meetings.headline: Superintendent warns prior budget cuts are pushing more students toward costly out-of-district special ed placements
meetings.summary: The committee heard a superintendent's report mixing a new DESE-funded reading tutoring grant with a warning that last year's cuts to in-district special education have left the district unable to serve some students, raising the risk of more out-of-district placements. The board discussed FY27 budget level-service figures, decided to stop applying for two small state family-engagement grants and hand them to a regional partner, voted to relocate meetings to the accessible middle-high school, gave the superintendent permission to explore redirecting a legislative earmark from passenger vans to ADA-accessible bathrooms at Turkey Hill, and heard principals describe strained staffing from prior cuts during school improvement plan updates.

meetings.board: School Committee Forum on the 2025 Budget Surplus
meetings.headline: School officials call the FY25 surplus a budgeting failure, not lost money, and warn FY27 will be tight
meetings.summary: School committee members, the superintendent, the business manager and the town manager held a public forum to explain how the district ended FY25 with an unexpectedly large surplus, attributing it mainly to a competitive grant that freed up already-budgeted paraprofessional funds that were never reallocated, plus austerity measures imposed on a mistaken sense of scarcity. No formal votes were taken; officials described new oversight practices already adopted (regular budget updates, grant pre-approval, a new stabilization fund for out-of-district placements) and residents pressed on transparency, MCAS reading scores, and whether another override will be needed.

Out-of-district placement costs vary widely year to year and can shock the budget when a child moves into town after the budget closes.

Inflation outpaced the maximum allowable tax levy increase over the period, described as the fundamental budget problem.
The district said it just learned from the state of an expected cut to Title I federal grant funding for the coming budget.
The special stabilization account for out-of-district costs is established but currently unfunded; the operating budget line it backstops was estimated at this figure.

minutes.headline: Town, school and finance officials agree Lunenburg likely needs a property-tax override to close a large FY27 budget gap
minutes.summary: This joint "tri-board" meeting of the Select Board, School Committee and Finance Committee opened with extensive public comment from firefighters and school staff describing understaffing and burnout, followed by a Town Manager presentation showing updated state aid and revenue figures leaving a large projected FY27 deficit once health insurance, retirement, transportation and a fourth fire shift are covered. The boards debated how to communicate the gap without "scare tactics," discussed override structures and cost-saving options (recycling, school choice, mosquito control), sparred over whether school staffing has actually been cut, and set a February 9th follow-up meeting without settling on an override amount.

what_happened.line: Town, school and finance officials agreed Lunenburg likely needs a property-tax override to close a projected FY27 gap, without settling on an amount or structure
The Town Manager walked the boards from updated state aid down through health insurance, retirement, transportation and a fourth fire shift to a remaining deficit
Finance and school committee members disputed whether district staffing has actually been cut, and the school committee agreed to supply updated data including last year's layoffs
The boards agreed to seek the state's override-options guidance and campaign-finance rules before any public campaign, and set a joint follow-up for February 9th

why_it_matters: If the boards move forward, residents would eventually vote on an override, which raises the property tax bill outside the normal levy limit -- and the town's April 10th ballot deadline is setting the pace of these discussions.

The named cost drivers -- health insurance, the county retirement assessment, transportation, and a fourth fire shift -- were described as largely fixed, meaning any budget relief this year would have to come from elsewhere or from new revenue.

The unresolved dispute over whether school staffing has grown or been cut touches what positions and services the school budget can protect, and residents will be asked to weigh that when an override figure is presented.

meetings.headline: Officials warn the FY27 budget leaves almost nothing after health insurance, pointing toward an override
meetings.summary: This was a joint Select Board / Finance Committee / School Committee ("tri-board") session in which the Town Manager walked through preliminary FY27 general government, debt, intergovernmental and revenue figures, including a new assistant town manager position, a large Munis/IT cost increase, and a steep audit-cost jump. The revenue walk-through showed that after health insurance is covered, almost no new money is left to fund any raises, cuts, or level services, and the group spent the second half of the meeting discussing operational efficiencies, the state and federal funding picture, and the likelihood that an override will be needed, without taking any substantive vote.

minutes.summary: The committee voted to put a special reserve fund for unbudgeted out-of-district special education and transportation costs on the November town meeting warrant, approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, and heard quarterly budget, athletics, and facilities reports. After extended debate, a second proposed warrant article to immediately appropriate roughly $22,185 in additional Chapter 70 funding was withdrawn in favor of seeking it through the regular FY27 budget process, and a proposal for an outside comprehensive/forensic audit of FY25 finances was deferred pending further talks with the town manager; the committee also discussed what to do about football and soccer uniforms that had been purchased without proper authorization.

The committee approved two new paraprofessional positions and restoring a full-time IT support position, both drawn from the salary reserve line.

Football and soccer uniforms bought without required purchase-order approval will not be penalized retroactively; undistributed soccer uniforms will be held for next year's replacement rotation.

why_it_matters: The reserve fund is a warrant article residents will vote on at November town meeting; it would let year-end school budget surplus automatically cover special education placement and transportation costs that come in over budget.
Withdrawing the Chapter 70 warrant article means any additional state aid this year would not be spent immediately but would instead be weighed against other priorities in the FY27 budget process.

The unauthorized uniform purchases and the salary-reserve-funded hires prompted the committee to signal it will develop a policy requiring pre-approval before staff spend outside the certified budget.

meetings.summary: The School Committee's meeting centered on a newly discovered FY25 budget surplus of roughly $582,000 (about 2% of the budget), far above the district's normal cushion, which the chair and later the business manager attributed to poor financial oversight rather than known wrongdoing. The committee approved FY25 line-item transfers and a warrant, heard the superintendent's and building principals' start-of-year reports (including the first-day fire at the middle/high school), reviewed an FY27 budget timeline, and discussed a possible best-practices/forensic audit, a stabilization fund for out-of-district special education placements, and extra Chapter 70 money for a fall town meeting warrant article; several residents used public comment to press for accountability and clearer FY25-vs-FY26 budget transparency.

minutes.headline: District disclosed a roughly $582,000 unspent FY25 school surplus that went unnoticed and unbudgeted for.
minutes.summary: The School Committee's meeting centered on a newly discovered FY25 budget surplus of roughly $582,000 (about 2% of the budget), far above the district's normal cushion, which the chair and later the business manager attributed to poor financial oversight rather than known wrongdoing. The committee approved FY25 line-item transfers and a warrant, heard the superintendent's and building principals' start-of-year reports (including the first-day fire at the middle/high school), reviewed an FY27 budget timeline, and discussed a possible best-practices/forensic audit, a stabilization fund for out-of-district special education placements, and extra Chapter 70 money for a fall town meeting warrant article; several residents used public comment to press for accountability and clearer FY25-vs-FY26 budget transparency.

what_happened.line: The chair disclosed a school budget surplus described as far larger than the district's normal cushion, calling it unbudgeted and unnoticed.
The committee voted to approve five FY25 line-item transfers, shifting money between accounts including athletics, stipends, and building maintenance to cover shortfalls.
Members and the business manager questioned whether paraprofessional positions were funded both in the general fund and against a federal special education grant.
Rather than vote, the committee put off a decision on a forensic or best-practices audit of FY25 and FY26 finances, asking the chair to bring back scope and possible RFP language next meeting.
The committee voted to approve a proposed FY27 budget development timeline.

why_it_matters: How the surplus was found and explained bears on trust in the budget process residents rely on when they vote on overrides and town meeting articles.
Whether paraprofessional pay was counted twice, once in the district budget and once in a federal grant, could change the real size of the special education budget line taxpayers fund.
A possible audit and a proposed reserve fund for out-of-district special education placements would, if pursued, show up as future warrant articles at town meeting.

minutes.summary: This was the first joint Select Board/School Committee/Finance Committee "tri-board" meeting, run by an outside facilitator, covering the fire department's proposed fourth shift, possible consolidation of town/school facilities, HR, legal and IT services, departmental growth pressures (special education, federal grant cuts), and financial-management controls after a revolving account ran into deficit. No consolidation, budget, or staffing item was put to a vote; the boards agreed to keep exploring facilities, HR and legal consolidation, to hold future tri-board meetings at Town Hall broadcast live, and to hold a dedicated public listening session in late October rather than public comment at every meeting.

budget_items.what_was_said: Each new hire's uniform allowance is set by contract per year, added to the fourth-shift cost estimate.
A school committee member said the district's guaranteed legal cost last year was a certain figure, used to argue for combining town and school legal services.
A board member cited the town's flat-rate contract figure for its lawyer from the prior year, contrasted with the school's hourly labor-attorney arrangement.

budget_items.topic: Trash/recycling cost and proposed enterprise fund
budget_items.what_was_said: A member cited what the town currently pays per year for recycling and proposed shifting trash/recycling to a self-funded enterprise fund, with savings potentially redirected to fund the fire department's fourth shift.
The finance director said the town saw a premium increase from its carrier this past year and has been told to expect at least the same increase again next year.
A school committee member described the cost range of out-of-district special education placements as a reason to invest in in-district BCBA staffing instead.

The superintendent said elimination of certain federal title grants for professional development and multilingual learner education has been reported statewide, which will affect the district's budget and the governor's earmark allowances.

A member described turning a parks and recreation department in a prior town of employment from a deficit to a profit over three years as an argument for making Lunenburg's recreation director full-time.

The finance director said one school revolving account went into a significant deficit this past school year because no budget had been entered for it in the town's financial system, so overspending wasn't flagged.

decisions.decision: The boards agreed facilities-department consolidation is worth exploring as a longer-term (FY26-FY28) possibility, not part of the current budget cycle.
The group narrowed its consolidation exploration list to facilities, HR, and legal/buying-power, while treating IT consolidation as a hard no per the school side.

Rather than a public comment period at every tri-board meeting, the group agreed to hold a dedicated public listening session around the end of October and to invite email/survey input at each meeting.
The finance director and a select board member agreed to draft a prioritized list of financial best practices to bring back to the committee.
The superintendent said hiring a business manager is the district's top financial-management priority right now.
The finance committee and superintendent agreed to aim for quarterly meetings going forward to avoid budget-season surprises.
The next tri-board meeting was set for August 26th per the already-circulated draft schedule.
Future tri-board meetings will be held at Town Hall, set up without using the stage, and broadcast live, rather than at the adult activity center.

minutes.headline: Committee got dire FY27–FY28 budget forecasts and agreed to push for an override or other new revenue.
minutes.summary: This meeting was largely a retirement send-off for outgoing Superintendent Dr. Kate Burnham, with extended public and staff tributes, alongside routine year-end business (transfers, surplus declarations, a scholarship gift, and a preschool/special-education compliance update). what_happened.line: The committee accepted FY27 and FY28 projections showing gaps large enough to commit to seeking an override or other new revenue rather than cuts alone.

minutes.headline: Committee reorganized, passed a bus fee policy, and moved to seek a fall FY27 override to stop annual staff layoff threats.
minutes.summary: This was the School Committee's reorganization meeting: three new members were sworn in, officers (chair, vice chair, secretary) and all subcommittee/liaison assignments were elected, and several routine annual votes were taken, including adopting the bus transportation fee policy on its third read. Members also discussed pursuing an FY27 override at a fall special town meeting to end recurring spring layoff threats to staff, asked the superintendent for early budget projections, debated how health insurance costs are counted in the school budget, and resolved confusion over the new superintendent's finalized contract.

what_happened.line: The committee decided to reach out to town boards about seeking a fall special town meeting override to end the annual threat of spring staff layoffs.
Three new members were sworn in and the committee elected a chair, vice chair and secretary as part of its annual reorganization.
The committee adopted a new bus transportation fee policy on its third read, setting reduced and waived rates tied to lunch-assistance status.
A member argued the school budget looks larger relative to other town departments because it carries health insurance costs those budgets do not.
The superintendent agreed to deliver a level-services FY27 budget projection, excluding free-cash-funded positions, before the year's last meeting.

why_it_matters: An override, if it reaches a fall town meeting, would ask residents to approve taxes above the levy cap to fund the school budget rather than face layoffs each spring.
The bus fee policy sets what families pay to ride the bus, with reduced or waived fees tied to free/reduced lunch status and a cap for multiple children.
How health insurance is counted changes what any comparison of the school budget's share of town spending shows, without changing what is actually spent.
watch_next: Superintendent's level-services FY27/FY28 budget projection, due before the committee's last meeting of 2025
Response from the town manager, select board and finance committee chairs on a fall special town meeting override
