meetings.board: School Committee Special Meeting - Superintendent Interview McCormick
meetings.headline: School Committee interviewed superintendent finalist Timothy McCormack for 75 minutes; no hiring decision made
meetings.summary: The Lunenburg School Committee held a special meeting to conduct a 75-minute, 13-question finalist interview for superintendent with candidate Timothy McCormack, currently superintendent in North Brookfield. Questions covered his background, budget philosophy, hiring practices, student safety, staff culture, labor relations, a past personal-conduct disclosure, and handling of a Facebook controversy over a Turkey Hill hire; the meeting ended with McCormack's closing statement and a roll-call vote to adjourn, with no hiring decision made.

budget_items.what_was_said: A committee member asked how the candidate would reconcile adding new programs with the district having just had to cut its budget, noting the figure is now lower than first thought.
The candidate described state grant funding attached to the Project Lead the Way / STEM pathway, paid in an initial larger amount and smaller amounts in subsequent years.
The candidate said his district received grant funding from the 18 Foundation to support programs like Project Lead the Way.

budget_items.topic: Value of a high school diploma vs. college
budget_items.what_was_said: A committee member challenged the candidate on steering some students away from college, citing average earnings for a high school diploma holder.

budget_items.topic: Cost differential in hiring a more experienced teacher
budget_items.what_was_said: The candidate discussed hiring a more expensive, experienced candidate versus a cheaper one, saying a district must find budget room elsewhere if it pays more for a position.
The candidate said conversations with the finance committee have grown more difficult as the required share of net school spending covered by the town has dropped sharply.
The candidate said his current district saw a reduction in rural school aid for next year that a slight increase in Chapter 70 would not fully offset.
The candidate said losing this funding, which had subsidized salaries, forced hard decisions about which positions were needs versus nice-to-haves.
The candidate referenced roughly twenty-plus one-to-one or small-group instructional aides in his district and the ongoing need to support them.

budget_items.what_was_said: Conway described facing a budget gap at Pentucket that was closed partly by raising revenue through summer programming, expanded preschool, and increased facility rental income.
Conway said putting the transportation contract out to competitive bid brought the three-year contract cost down sharply once a competitor entered the bidding.
Conway called health insurance a major budget driver, citing recent rate increases well above typical assumed growth rates.
Conway explained that an approved September budget commonly looks different by year-end because of line transfers made to respond to changing needs, such as adding a kindergarten class.
Conway said UGGA has remained largely flat and argued that if it kept pace with Chapter 70 growth the town would have more budget flexibility.
Conway described a robotics program he built at Pentucket that runs on an annual budget funded largely by industry sponsorships and grants rather than district funds.

meetings.headline: Committee voted to swap FY26 capital projects for funds to finish a grant-funded mini-split project
meetings.summary: An emergency school committee meeting was called to decide whether to amend the FY26 capital plan, pulling several school capital projects (playground and driveway design studies, safety window film, and a Turkey Hill hot water tank replacement, among others) and replacing them with funding to complete phase two of the mini-split installation at the primary school, in order to use a Green Communities grant before it expires and free the town to apply for further grants. After extended discussion about the funding math, the abruptness of the request, and tradeoffs against deferred safety projects, the committee voted by roll call to endorse the town manager's and superintendent's plan to modify the capital plan request.

meetings.headline: School Committee passed a deeply-cut FY26 budget and created Lunenburg's first student transportation fee.
meetings.summary:
The School Committee worked through the superintendent's FY26 recommended budget line by line, confirming a Director of Finance restructuring, a cut to one of two curriculum coaches, and rejecting a proposed librarian cut, while extensive public comment focused on athletic and band cuts, the co-op ski program's cost, and equity between academics and extracurriculars. The committee voted to table a ski program cut pending renegotiation with partner schools, adopted a new student bus fee (with rates and a waiver policy sent to the policy subcommittee) to help offset transportation costs, and ultimately passed the FY26 budget unanimously with the ski program retained and funded by projected bus fee revenue; members also confirmed they will not pursue a school override this year in favor of a possible townwide override next year.</summary>

Reports covered MSBA updates, the town manager search narrowing to three finalists, a capital plan list likely to be well-funded due to extra free cash and ARPA offsets, and the concluded budget task force's presentation to the select board, including support for pursuing the Community Preservation Act.

meetings.headline: Building panel unveils ~$15M plan to move schools into Ritter, restore Town Hall; Turkey Hill's fate left open
meetings.summary: The Municipal Building Design Committee presented its plan to relocate school offices into the former Ritter library building, restore Town Hall as a community meeting house, and build a new administrative annex, while leaving Turkey Hill's future to a later school committee decision tied to an ongoing facilities study. The board also discussed the statewide elimination of the MCAS graduation requirement, weighed whether to adopt a district cell phone policy (referring it to school advisory councils), and reviewed calendar options for the December 2025 holiday break. Only the prior minutes and adjournment were formally voted on; other matters were discussion, reports, or informal direction.

meetings.headline: Committee skipped a vote, told the superintendent to submit turf-field drainage study and auditorium upgrades as its top ARPA asks
meetings.summary: The school committee spent most of this meeting deciding what to request from the town's remaining ARPA funds, reviewing a superintendent-prepared list of capital-type projects including a primary school generator, AC phase two, concession stand keycard access, auditorium booth upgrades, and a track/turf drainage study. Rather than vote, the committee reached consensus to prioritize the turf drainage study and the auditorium booth upgrades, drop the AC project from the list, and let the superintendent compile and submit the remainder for the select board's consideration. The committee also approved June 5 minutes, tabled two other sets of minutes pending corrections, and agreed to schedule an August meeting to act on the capital plan.

meetings.headline: School Committee approved the override-adjusted FY25 budget, with one member abstaining
meetings.summary: The committee finalized the FY25 budget as adjusted after the successful override, approved a $76,336 line-item transfer, and heard from a TMS consultant about ongoing MUNIS and accounting delays at Town Hall. It also debated the LHS activity fee's fairness, revisited the parent-teacher conference calendar, appointed a member to the town manager search committee, discussed a town payroll-timing change that could cause employees to miss a paycheck, and reviewed i-Ready assessment results showing strong K-5 progress and weaker middle-school results, before entering executive session.

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reported the warrant total for the period and asked if anyone had questions.

TMS consultant Paul Livingston explained a transfer moving money from psychologist salaries, fire safety and furniture repair lines to dues and fees, transportation, computer purchase/lease, and water charges, because psychologist positions could not be filled and a contracted service was used instead.
A one-year, 2.5% increase was proposed for unaffiliated staff, mostly extended-day program employees paid from a revolving account, with minimal budget impact.

All high school students pay a mandatory annual activity fee funding guest speakers, advisor stipends, Science Olympiad, graduation/homecoming supplies and some field trip bus costs; students who don't pay cannot graduate. The board discussed whether it is fair as a mandatory, non-optional fee.
Middle school clubs such as ski club and Science Olympiad charge a per-club fee covering supplies, registration and some transportation.
Turkey Hill charges a fee for after-school activities, funding teacher stipends and materials for a roughly five-week session.
The primary school charges a similar fee for its after-school activity sessions, funding stipends and materials.

The committee discussed returning ARPA funds to the town for reappropriation by the select board, consistent with what was represented at town meeting, and asked to be part of future discussions on how the money is reused.

budget_items.topic: Maintenance of buildings contracted services line
budget_items.what_was_said: This line was discussed relative to the prior year's figure and the current budget figure after removing E911 compliance costs intended to be funded through ARPA.
A one-time E911 compliance cost was discussed as possibly funded through ARPA or state earmark funds; there was uncertainty whether an earmark would come through.
A public safety training system fell just below the funding line on the capital plan; a member expressed support for finding a way to fund it.
The out-of-district/private special education tuition line was funded at a stated amount, adjusted based on newly known student needs.
This line was adjusted due to a transition between IEP software systems.
The curriculum adoption line was reduced as part of budget line adjustments.

budget_items.topic: Primary school math supplies / library books
budget_items.what_was_said: These lines were reduced after principals were told they could spend down current-year budget lines that had been frozen.
The special education transportation line was increased to reflect newly known added students requiring transportation.

The committee voted to approve the total budget reflecting the override, adjusted from the earlier 'pink' budget for updated salaries and grant offsets, with one member abstaining due to insufficient review time.

The chair reported Chapter 70 came in higher than expected for Lunenburg and said she needed to ask the state representative where the additional amount came from, given the district is not a hold-harmless district.

budget_items.topic: Town payroll timing change / overtime pay
budget_items.what_was_said: Members objected to a planned change in town payroll timing that could cause employees, including lower-wage workers, to miss a paycheck by about a week; they asked for cost details on mitigation options such as a special check.

The LHS activity fee and related fee structure will be revisited as a fall agenda item before the FY26 budget process begins, with the superintendent researching how other districts handle similar fees.
The committee will work to schedule the legislative delegation meeting for the fall rather than immediately, given the state budget process has largely concluded for this cycle.
The June 26th meeting will be held remotely via Zoom given member availability.

meetings.headline: Override passed, giving Lunenburg schools level-service funding but no expansion as ESSER funds end
meetings.summary: This School Committee meeting was largely a post-override celebration and reporting session: public comment and the chair's report thanked voters, staff, and advocates for the town's successful override vote, which will level-fund schools (offsetting expiring ESSER money) without expanding programs. The committee voted to reject a proposed rainwater retention/stormwater demonstration project at the middle-high school after learning it was sited without consulting the district and had already cost several thousand dollars in engineering, and voted not to increase school choice seats to protect small class sizes; it also received presentations on a new family-school partnership compact, the state's new IEP form, and facilities project updates.

attendees.role: special education staff, presenter (team chair/school psychologist)

budget_items.what_was_said: The chair reported a legislative bill sponsored by MASC, MASS, MTA and AFT that would apply an inflation adjustment to Chapter 70; a MASC representative told her it would bring Lunenburg new funding if passed.

The chair said the town is not a held-harmless community; it got a small percentage increase last year after its low-income count rose, which is more than held-harmless towns get but far less than other communities receive.

budget_items.topic: Circuit breaker reimbursement rate / proposed 100% bill
budget_items.what_was_said: Committee discussed a bill proposing 100% reimbursement of special education circuit-breaker costs; a member clarified the current formula reimburses after districts cover four times foundation, and there is confusion whether the bill means 100% of the current 75% rate or a new 100% rate.
The chair reported the amount of warrants signed for the period, directing questions to the superintendent's office.
A committee member asked how much was spent designing the stormwater BMP without consulting the school district first; the presenter estimated the range for the engineering design work.
The chair said a legislator has been pushing for an earmark tied to enhanced 911 funding for the town that could come through now that the override passed.

budget_items.what_was_said: A check from Box Tops for Education was recommended for acceptance into the primary school's gift account, to support upcoming school trips.

budget_items.what_was_said: A second Box Tops for Education check was recommended for acceptance into the Turkey Hill Elementary gift account.

A speaker explained the override was set at the modest amount needed to level-fund schools versus the prior year minus expiring ESSER funds, not to expand programs; some positions will still be cut as planned.
The chair noted the state's millionaire's tax has collected more revenue than expected, which legislators are looking to direct toward education and transportation.
A speaker thanked everyone who participated in the town vote on the override.

decisions.decision: Superintendent will have the business/facilities staff prepare an informational slide deck on student activity fees for a June meeting.
Committee members agreed to send the chair proposed topics for the legislative delegation before the next meeting so a combined session can be scheduled.
A building/facility maintenance plan will be added to the committee's list of goals but is not expected soon given the facilities director's current workload.
Completed superintendent evaluations are due to be submitted by June 5th ahead of the June 12th meeting.
Committee agreed to place ARPA funds, which some feel should be returned, on a future agenda for discussion.

meetings.summary: The meeting centered on finalizing a public communication plan for the school budget override before town meeting: a statement drafted by the chair, a "dry run" presentation planned for the next meeting, and grassroots support ideas like blue ribbons, alongside frank internal debate over whether the committee communicates well with the public.
